News.title: David Lammy gave the PM the phone number of the con artist pretending to be Donald Trump’s aide
News.content:
The PM fell for a hoaxer pretending to be one of Donald Trump's most powerful aides

HOAX CALL David Lammy gave the PM the phone number of the con artist pretending to be Donald Trump’s aide

DAVID Lammy gave the PM the phone number of the con artist pretending to be Donald Trump’s chief-of-staff, The Sun on Sunday can reveal.

Andy Burnham exchanged several messages with someone pretending to be Susie Wiles – one of the most powerful figures in Washington.



It was a major security gaffe by the new No10 regime and the British embassy had to admit their blunder to the White House.

We can reveal that it was Mr Lammy who gave the bogus number to Mr Burnham, believing it to be genuine.



It suggests that it was the PM who first made the contact.

A source said: “David Lammy thought he was currying favour with the new PM by getting them the phone number of one of the most powerful people in Washington.

“But it turned out to be the wrong one and the whole thing has turned into a massive headache for the PM.

“It is a serious embarrassment for David.”

Mr Lammy had boasted of his close ties with the Trump administration when he was deputy PM under Sir Keir Starmer.

He made much of his friendship with Vice President JD Vance, even taking President Trump’s deputy fishing at his then grace-and-favour home Chevening House.



The blunder with the bogus number is a major embarrassment for Mr Lammy, who was sacked from the Cabinet when Mr Burnham became PM.

Downing Street has said only a handful of messages were exchanged and they contained nothing significant.

But they have refused to give details about exactly what was in the message and when they were sent.

Quizzed on the blunder earlier this week, the PM denied he was embarrassed by the gaffe.



Mr Burnham said: “No, I am not because there was a minimal exchange, nothing of consequence and quickly I realised that this needed to be reported and I did so.

“So I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right.”

Ms Wiles is one of President Trump’s most trusted and senior aides.

Her personal phone was hacked in May last year, sparking an FBI probe.

But the White House said the latest incident had “nothing to do” with Ms Wiles’ phone being hacked.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

When approached by The Sun on Sunday, Mr Lammy’s team said it would not be appropriate to comment on matters relating to national security .

No10 also declined to comment.

News.title: Putin says Ukraine opened ‘Pandora’s box’ with strikes on Russia’s ‘Amazon’ and vows to hit back
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin has accused Volodymyr Zelensky of opening “Pandora’s box” with strikes on oil refineries and retailers.

The Kremlin has responded – including with attacks on ⁠grain exports via the Black Sea – and the Russian President has further threatened Ukraine‘s “most sensitive economic sectors,” which he said are “already on their last legs”.



“The Kyiv regime set out ​to ⁠damage our economy,” he told journalist Pavel Zarubin. “What ‌did it do? It opened this Pandora’s box itself.

“[They will] get an answer about the most sensitive economic sector… they are frankly already on their last legs.



“This, incidentally, also applies to agricultural production, the export of which is the Kyiv regime’s main source of income.”

Putin claimed that Ukraine’s strikes have had “no impact” on the frontline and that Russian soldiers have ramped up “the pace of their advance”.

For weeks, drones have pummelled Russia, stretching from Moscow and St Petersburg, to cities in the south, and eastward to the Ural Mountains.

Targets have included oil refineries and warehouses belonging to Russia’s Wildberries, burning billions of dollars’ worth of merchandise and bringing the war home to the broad public.



Earlier today, Ukraine also hit a site owned by online retailer Ozon, Russia’s second largest retailer – for the first time – as well as an industrial facility.

Russian officials said that 10 people were killed in the strike.

Ukraine sees strikes on facilities like Ozon as a legitimate target to kill anything feeding the Russian war economy.



Elsewhere, in the southern region of Krasnodar, three people, two of them children, were killed and another adult was wounded in a strike on the Sea of Azov port town of Yeysk.

This comes just hours after 16 people were killed and 130 wounded as two Russian drones smashed into a busy shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih in quick succession in what is known as a double-tap strike.

Rescuers are still digging through the smoking debris in their search for survivors. Four people remain missing.

Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha revealed that 22 children are among the injured in the daytime attack on the city.

“There are 29 people ​in ⁠serious condition, including five children,” he said.



Zelensky called the attack “absolutely cynical and despicable” in a post on Telegram.

“The attack drones struck in two waves: half an hour after the first strike and the resulting fire, there was a second strike targeting emergency responders,” he said.

“Attacks like these are nothing less than ⁠terrorist acts. We will definitely respond.”

News.title: Moment police cars pursue suspect in high-speed chase three minutes before 7 including two cops killed in horror crash
News.content:
THIS is the moment three police cars pursue a suspect down a narrow residential road in a high speed chase – just minutes before seven people died in a horror crash.

Two brave gun cops – PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38 – were killed after their vehicle collided with a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 near Middlesbrough in the early hours.



Chilling Ring doorbell footage obtained by The Sun on Sunday captured the Passat tearing down a residential street.

Minutes later, the Passat is understood to have been racing the wrong way down the A-road when it collided with two serving officers driving the other way in a marked cop car.



The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said officers gave chase in the early hours after identifying the Passat as a “suspicious vehicle”.

Three police cars, with their blue lights flashing and sirens wailing, followed at speed as the vehicle headed towards the arterial road where the crash occurred.

The Passat shot down Lime Road in Teesville, Middlesbrough, at 3.36am on its way towards the A66.

Residents said they were woken at 3:36am by the sound of screeching tyres as the motor took a corner into their narrow street.



Ellie Westerman, 24, said: “The car must have been travelling at between 80 and 100 mph down our narrow street.

“The noise woke me and I shot out of bed, you could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going.

“It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area and it’s tragic people have ended up dying.”

Another resident said: “The screech of tyres woke me up, the car being followed must have taken the corner into our road at a tremendous speed.”

Local resident Neil Hutchinson, 47, said: “The police cars were tearing down the street at half past three with lights flashing and their sirens going,



“You could tell from the noise that they were travelling at high speed.

“Two cars went down the street and then a few seconds later there was a third.

“They were obviously going after another vehicle.



“It’s a narrow street with cars parked on either side so it must have been a serious situation to be going at that speed down this road.”

Sadly, all occupants of the vehicles were declared dead at the scene.

A referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The IOPC said it is believed the officers spotted a suspicious vehicle and began a pursuit.

The car then travelled onto the A66 and collided with the police car.



The A66 will stay closed between Normanby Road and Church Lane for some time Cleveland Police have said.

Chief Constable Victoria Fuller Their devastated Chief Constable Victoria Fuller fought back tears as she spoke of their “unimaginable loss”.

She said: “First and foremost, our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in today’s incident.

“No one should leave their home and not return safely, including police officers serving their communities and protecting the people of Cleveland.

“This tragic incident will be felt across Cleveland, within our communities and throughout the entire policing family.



“We are providing specialist support to all families involved at this extremely difficult time.

“The investigation has been referred to the IOPC, which is the standard approach when a death occurs following police contact. We will cooperate fully with their investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“While this investigation takes place, we strongly urge people to avoid speculation.”

The families of those identified have been informed and are being offered specialist support.

News.title: I cut dad out after brutal attack on my twin before he died… he has sent creepy notes for years – I fear he’ll find me
News.content:
ABI Early held her breath and opened the card – the strong smell of aftershave filling the room and making her feel sick.

Twice a year, like clockwork, Gavin Gibbs would send a card and a present for his daughter’s birthday and at Christmas, and it became a nightmarish reminder of what he’d done to her tragic twin brother.





Thug Gibbs was jailed for a vicious attack on three-month-old Charlie, described by a judge as an “appalling act of violence”, before the little tot died.

Gibbs, a paramedic, had initially been charged with murder, his son having sustained catastrophic injuries, including to his brain over a number of weeks – but he only served 11 months in prison for GBH. He was found not guilty of murder.

Abi, now 18, never knew her dad – who she and her mum Jo Early refuse to name, instead calling him Voldemort after Harry Potter’s archvillain – but by law he retained parental responsibility for her, which would include rights to access and control over certain aspects of her life.

Jo took her ex-husband Gibbs to family court on his release from prison and he ultimately agreed to give up his legal rights in exchange for a list of demands, including entitling him to Abi’s school and medical reports, photos, and being notified if she planned to go abroad.

As part of the agreement, in place up to her turning 16, it was also agreed he could send her cards and presents on her birthday and at Christmas.

Abi spoke exclusively to The Sun as part of a joint campaign with her mum Jo to get the law changed to restrict automatic parental responsibility in such cases.

She said: “If I had it my way, I would have chosen never to have had any contact with him – direct or indirect.

“I don’t want anything to do with him.”





Abi recalls initially having conflicted feelings about her dad and why he wasn’t around, feeling jealous of her school pals who had both parents at home.

But from around the age of 10 or 11, she’d begun to realise the horrible truth.

“Before that, I had barely any understanding of it,” she said. “I knew my brother was no longer here and my dad was a bad man. That was it.”

Abi can’t pinpoint the age she first opened a card from her dad, admitting: “I’ve blocked most of it out because I’m traumatised by it.”

But she recalls: “One of the cards said something along the lines of, because it was Christmas time, ‘hope you’ve been a good girl and Santa gives you lots of presents’.”

As a younger child, Gibbs would also send her presents like Teddy bears, but she can’t remember that.

“I just remember there was always a voucher with the card,” she said. “I’ve never spent them, out of spite. I just don’t want his money.”

But the most haunting part for Abi is smelling her dad’s aftershave in the cards.



“It’s really nasty and I’ll never forget the smell of that aftershave. It actually haunts me,” she said.

“I’d always hold my breath. I’d get a little whiff and I was like, no, I just couldn’t do it.”

As she grew up, birthdays and Christmases became a cruel waiting game for when her dad’s cards arrived.

“I’d be like, I know what’s coming in the next few days,” she said. “I didn’t want to deal with them, but I’d open them anyway because it’s natural curiosity.”

Then, things took a darker turn.

The family court agreement prevented Gibbs making direct contact with Abi outside of the cards until she was 16.

But on her 16th birthday on July 23, 2024, Abi received a text from an unknown number and on opening it her heart skipped a beat.

“We’re still kind of confused as to how he got my number,” she said.



Jo had left where they’d lived in Kent and moved across the country when Abi was very young, and Gibbs has never known exactly where.

But receiving that text made it seem like the distance between them was closing in.

“The fact that he thought it was acceptable to message me blew my mind,” said Abi.

“At the bottom of the message it said, ‘if you choose to block me, it will be your choice’.

“So, I think he knew that doing it was wrong. I think he was just trying it on a little bit. I still have the message. It’s very long.”

She explained: “It was mostly him talking about how he wishes this situation could change and things like that. It’s all about him.”

Abi ultimately responded and told him never to contact her again.

“I’ve never had a ‘sorry’ from him,” she said. “It’s all narcissism.”



But the message brought to the fore Abi and Jo’s biggest fear, now that she’s an adult.

“I worry that he’s going to find out where I live and knock on my door,” said Abi. “All the time.”

The cards and presents from Gibbs were always sent via his parents and collected by Jo to pass to her daughter.

“He’s never known my address,” said Abi who believes he went through his late mum’s phone for her number.

“Growing up, if I was having a sleepover with a friend, I’d always be cautious about giving my address in case they’d leak it and he would find out where I lived,” she explained.

“And I still have that worry. I’m always going to have that worry.”

Since Abi’s 18th birthday last month, she and Jo have begun a campaign to change the law, with the teenager admitting she is now Charlie’s “voice”.

“A lot of my friends have grown up with siblings and I haven’t, and I should have,” she said. “And it is hard for me to think about what he would have been like as a person.



“So, I just generally tend to not think about it.”

Jo and Gibbs welcomed Charlie and Abi on July 23, 2008 and couldn’t be happier with their growing family.

They’d met while both working for the London Ambulance Service and been together for seven years, with Jo, a control room operative, describing Gibbs as the “life and soul of the party”.

But Gibbs had a rage inside him that Jo never saw coming and it would tear the family apart.

“I had to accept that he had this whole other side to him,”Jo, 54, told The Sun.

On his release from prison after just 11 months, she added: “I don’t think we got any justice at all.”

On October 23 2008, when the twins were three months old, baby Abi was admitted to Queen Mary’s Hospital, Sidcup, with bronchiolitis.

Jo had gone with her, while Gibbs stayed at home with Charlie.

That night, as she drifted off to sleep next to Abi, she was told by a nurse there was a call for her – it was an ambulance crew mate of Gibbs’ telling her little Charlie was downstairs in A&E and he’d stopped breathing.

He was quickly transferred to Kings College hospital in Camberwell, South London, and over the next few hours the mum faced a barrage of questions.



She said: “I was thinking, why are they being so horrible?”

X-rays and other tests would show Charlie had not only suffered a fatal brain injury, but also a severely broken left arm and a series of older fractures, including to a rib, ankle and his skull.

Jo explained: “They said, ‘what’s happened to him?’ I said ‘what are you talking about? No one has dropped him, I would know.’

“I just thought it was a medical problem and everyone had got it horribly wrong.”

Charlie was kept on life support for two days before being declared brain dead.

Jo and Gibbs then went to his bedside and as he passed away, the dad leant over his son to say “please forgive me”.

But still the doting mum could not bring herself to believe her partner would do anything to harm their kids.

“I had no inclination as to what he’d done,” she said.

Gibbs was arrested but wasn’t charged for almost 13 months, and then applied for bail that allowed him out of custody on remand while he awaited a trial for murder.

Soon after, having had a meeting with his solicitor, on December 1 2009 Gibbs finally opened up to Jo.



“He said ‘I’ve got something to tell you’,” she explained.

“‘Two weeks before Charlie died, he fell off the sofa and it caused a fracture.’”

Jo was gobsmacked. He’d claimed before he’d known nothing about their son’s injuries.

“I looked at him and just felt myself go really cold,” she said. “That was the moment of realisation that I’d got it completely wrong and everyone else was right.”

She continued: “I just thought, I need to leave this house right now and never come back. And that’s what I did. I never spoke to him again after that.”

She admitted: “There’s a shame you have as a mother.

“Injuries in babies aren’t always obvious… but you blame yourself because you think I should have known. Other mums I’ve spoken to have said the same.”

In 2010, Gibbs was put on trial at the Old Bailey but jurors acquitted him of murder.

Instead, he was convicted of grievous bodily harm for an incident 17 days prior to the baby’s death, where he’d deliberately twisted and broke his arm, and sentenced to three years in prison.

However, Gibbs launched a successful legal appeal and his sentence was reduced to two years, and he went on to serve just 11 months in custody.



Psychologists had advised Jo to drip feed the information about Gibbs and Charlie to Abi as she grew up.

She explained that the experts told her “don’t sugar coat it”.

“Don’t lie because she’ll find out – it’s a trust thing. Just give her little bits at a time and the story grows with her,” Jo explained.

“It’s difficult telling a child the reality of what’s happened when you know it’s going to have an impact on them.

“But we can’t escape from it. It’s a life sentence for us.”

She continued: “We can’t even say his name without feeling sick – it’s really hard.

“We call him Voldemort – from Harry Potter.”

As part of their Charlie’s Law campaign, Jo and Abi are now calling for parents who murder or cause serious harm to their children to automatically lose parental responsibility in the Courts and Tribunals Bill currently going through parliament or in a separate act.

Click here to see their petition.

News.title: Five passengers injured as laptop suddenly catches fire in cabin mid-flight on packed American Airlines plane
News.content:
PLANE DRAMA Five passengers injured as laptop suddenly catches fire in cabin mid-flight on packed American Airlines plane

FIVE people have suffered burns after a laptop burst into flames inside the cabin on a crowded American Airlines flight.

Passengers were injured after a device caught fire shortly before landing on a flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas.



It is understood the laptop burst into flames inside the cabin at the rear of the plane on Friday.

There were 133 passengers on board at the time.



In audio obtained by CBS News, the pilot can be heard reporting the incident to air traffic control.

He said: “Cabin fire in the back of the airplane.



“The flight attendants are trying to put it out now.”

“I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop.”

The plane made a safe landing and emergency workers were waiting on the ground to care for the passengers, with one requiring medical attention, BBC reported.

According to CBS, American Airlines said: “American Airlines flight 2398 landed safely at DFW after reports of smoke from a customer’s device during landing.



“We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device.”

The FAA warns that laptop and phone lithium batteries risk dangerous overheating on flights through “thermal runaway.”

They said: “Thermal runaway can occur without warning as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed.”

There are size limits for lithium batteries on flights because of those risks.

This year, there have been at least 56 lithium battery incidents reported on flights that involved smoke, fire or overheating, according to FAA.



It comes as American Airlines narrowly avoided a mid-air collision after two planes were were unknowingly cruising under identical flight numbers.

The error meant the two planes were on course to crash into each other.

The impending crisis was scarcely averted after one eagle-eyed air traffic controller spotted the mix-up and leapt into action.

In a statement to The Sun, American Airlines said: “We are reviewing ​the ​details ​related ​to ​two American ​flights with the same ​call sign near ​Phoenix ​(PHX) ​around ​midnight ​on Aug. 14.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The diligence ​and professionalism ​of air ​traffic controllers ​and our ​pilots ​ensured ​required separation was always maintained ​and the ​issue ​was ​identified and ​addressed.



“Both flights ​continued safely and ​without incident.”

News.title: Andy Burnham must cut welfare and public spending or he will be punished by the market
News.content:
Respected economist Gerard Lyons as the new PM faces a choice in his Budget in October: cut sky-high public spending or face more economic turmoil

GERARD LYONS Andy Burnham must cut welfare and public spending or he will be punished by the market

WATCH what he does, don’t just listen to what he says. That will be the lesson of the next few months as Andy Burnham unveils his Government’s economic plans.

In September Burnham gives his first speech as Prime Minister to the Labour Party Conference. Then in late October Chancellor John Healey delivers the Budget.

Britain needs to make a clear choice about the direction of economic policy. The stakes are high.



The economy grew solidly in the first half of the year, helped by AI boosting productivity.



But confidence is low. Energy and business costs are high, living standards are being squeezed and people fear taxes will rise.

Last week borrowing rates rose across the globe. It’s not just governments that are borrowing heavily.

Now the AI boom is leading big tech firms to borrow to finance their plans. This is pushing borrowing rates higher for everyone.



Britain is particularly exposed. Inflation remains persistent. And international investors are concerned about public spending and whether Burnham and Healey can make their fiscal sums add up.

There are two UK policy paths ahead. The danger is that Burnham takes us down the one his party faithful want to hear, rather than the one the economy needs.

That means a bigger state. More public spending. And ultimately higher taxes or more borrowing.



Burnham talks of reversing Thatcherism. Yet much of what Thatcher achieved on the public finances has already been reversed.

Public spending was just under 40 per cent of GDP when she left office. Britain was also seen as open for business, with policy aimed at incentivising the private sector.

Today public spending is 45 per cent of GDP and rising. Spending is around £1.4 trillion. The national debt is £2.99 trillion, up £96 billion over the last year.

We now spend almost as much on welfare as we collect in income tax. Welfare provides an essential safety net. But it needs to be better targeted and brought under control.

More than half of households get more back from the state than they pay in taxes. And this isn’t just about pensioners. Among non-retired households the figure is 46 per cent.



Two other big themes of Burnham’s agenda are investment and devolution. Both have attractions but neither ensures success.

Britain has invested too little for decades. But investment is not automatically productive. What matters is what you invest in, what it costs and what return it produces. HS2 should be warning enough.

Likewise devolution. Taking decisions closer to the people they affect makes sense.

But greater power should come with financial responsibility. Otherwise taxpayers nationally pick up the bill when things go wrong.

All of this has to be paid for in the Budget. Last year’s Budget rebuilt the fiscal buffer to £21.7 billion. This is the shock absorber that still allows the fiscal rules to be met.



It has since fallen below £10 billion. This Budget needs to rebuild the buffer while finding extra money for welfare, investment and defence.

There are only so many ways to make the sums add up. Faster growth is the best. But that’s not guaranteed.

Without it the choices are public sector reform, spending restraint, higher taxes or more borrowing.

Public sector reform is difficult and takes time. Spending restraint is clearly not planned. Borrowing is already high.



That leaves more taxes. But the tax take is already at an all-time high. The lessons from abroad are that wealth taxes don’t work and end up hitting the middle class. The housing market is stagnating as property is already heavily taxed.

Incentives matter. Bond markets won’t be fooled by tax increases that deliver little revenue or hit future growth.

There is another path.

Don’t make things worse by spending more public money we don’t have. If markets lose confidence the consequences could be a weaker pound, rising interest rates and higher borrowing costs, hitting business hard.

Remove barriers to growth that don’t cost money. Ease unnecessary regulation on small and medium-sized firms and reform planning.



Cutting energy costs is critical while delivering the green agenda, but it requires investment.

Above all, put the public finances on a sounder footing. Control spending and reform welfare.

And mobilise private capital. Banks are awash with capital and liquidity. The City should do more to channel this into infrastructure and productive investment rather than assuming every ambition requires Government spending.

Burnham has political capital. He can use it to expand the state further or confront the structural problems holding Britain back.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One path means more spending, higher taxes and a bigger state. The other means fiscal discipline, reform and creating the conditions for the private economy to grow.



If the Government is unwilling to make that choice, the markets will ultimately make it for them.

News.title: Haunting last three words Lindsay Clancy said to three-year-old son as ‘psychotic’ mom strangled him
News.content:
LINDSAY Clancy said three haunting final words to her son as she strangled him, a psychiatrist revealed to jurors.

The revelation was made in court on Friday as the defense rested its case which attempted to convince jurors the 36-year-old mom is not criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children due to her mental state.



On January 24, 2023, her husband Patrick came home from running errands to find Clancy lying injured outside under their bedroom window, and their three children dead in the basement of their Massachusetts home.

Five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan had been strangled with exercise bands by their mother, who was allegedly suffering from undiagnosed postpartum psychosis.





As the defense wrapped up the gruelling four-week trial, prosecutors called on forensic psychiatrist Dr. Avram Mack for their rebuttal.

He told the court what Clancy told him about the day she killed her three children and tried to kill herself in a botched suicide attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down.

“First she took Dawson down to the basement,” and wrapped an elastic exercise band around his neck, Mack testified.

“While that was happening she was saying out loud, ‘Go to God.'”



He further added that the Catholic mom said similar phrases while killing her other two children.

“My understanding is that the sentiment ‘Go to God’ is a way of bestowing or thinking about the children as innocents, as ones who hadn’t done wrong while what she was doing was the opposite, was wrong or could be construed as wrong,” Mack said.

“‘Go to God’ not only was a hope for the children but a description of the situation.”

He had previously testified that Clancy told him a male voice instructed her to kill the children and then herself but that she carried out her crimes “methodically” knowing that it was wrong.



Meanwhile, the final witness called on Friday for the defense was Dr. Phillip Resnick, another forensic psychiatrist and expert in the killing of a child by a parent.

He testified that Clancy was “clearly psychotic” and that “it was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings.”

Resnick further said that in his hours of interviews with Clancy over four months after the murders, she would try to minimize her mental health symptoms rather than make them sound worse than they were.

He said she suffered from severe depression and showed symptoms in line with bipolar disorder.



According to the medical expert, she was experienced a “command hallucination” and “delusion of influence” on the day she killed the children.

“My opinion is that Ms Clancy was, due to her mental disease, unable to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law on the day that she took the lives of her children,” Resnick told jurors.

Closing arguments are set to be heard next week with jurors returning to court on Monday morning around 9am.

The harrowing trial which has dragged on for almost a month has seen the mother give several gut- wrenching reactions as she was forced to her testimony and evidence about the brutal deaths of her children.

On one occasion she broke down in tears and cried out “I can’t do this” as medical examiners described the injuries inflicted on the kids.



Another heavily watched moment came when Patrick entered the courtroom to testify, reportedly the first time Lindsay had seen him since the night their children died.

Meanwhile, Clancy’s defense attorney Kevin Reddington has had some fiery trial moments which you can watch here on The U.S. Sun’s youtube channel.

Also see our exclusive interview revealing why he was met with a pink-clad wall of silence when he arrived at court.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.

News.title: Millions of mailboxes across US fill up with ‘one-time’ payment from $5bn State Farm payout as checks start arriving
News.content:
CASH IN Millions of mailboxes across US fill up with ‘one-time’ payment from $5bn State Farm payout as checks start arriving

A MAJOR insurance company is shelling out a historic $5 billion one-time dividends payout to millions of eligible customers.

America’s largest auto insurer, State Farm, recently announced the multi-billion dollar payment payout – the largest in the company’s history.

The company boasts over 49 million insurance clients – many of whom will have been eligible for a chunk of money.



State Farm says several million have already received their money and remaining dividends will be sent out in the next few months.



The company said the dividend is possible thanks to the “financial strength” and “stronger than expected underwriting performance in 2025.”

State Farm is a mutual insurance company, which means policyholders have the chance to share in the company’s yearly profits through dividends.

Mutual President and Executive Director Jon Farney said: “As a mutual [insurance] company with a customer-centered focus, State Farm Mutual can contribute direct value to our customers and simultaneously maintain the financial strength necessary to fulfill our future promises.

“This year, this translated to lower auto payments and cash returns in the form of $5 billion in dividends for those insured.”

Clients who meet the requirements will be notified about the payment either via email or physical mail.

State Farm Mutual will send payments to customers with an active auto insurance policy between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2025.

The minimum payment required for processing is $10.



Customers who had State Farm policies in 2025 but no longer do so still may be eligible for payouts.

The payment process is forecast to take months to complete across the country.

Policies issued by a state-assigned risk program do not qualify.

It comes as AAA insurance paid $4.5 million to settle claims that it wrongly reduced uninsured motorist payouts by the amount paid by the at-fault driver.

Affected drivers were able to apply for claims up to $25,000 back in May.

News.title: Japan earthquake measuring magnitude 5.9 shakes Tokyo and eastern Kanto region
News.content:
Japan earthquake measuring magnitude 5.9 shakes Tokyo and eastern Kanto region

A 5.9-magnitude earthquake shook Tokyo and the eastern Kanto region in Japan in the early hours of Sunday local time

View 2 Images A 5.9-magnitude earthquake struck Japan (Image: Japan Meteorological Agency )

A 5.9-magnitude earthquake has rattled Tokyo and the eastern Kanto region in Japan.

‌



The quake struck southern Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 43 miles (70km) at around 6pm BST on Saturday (2am local time on Sunday). The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) recorded a lower 5 on Japan's seven-level seismic intensity scale in Adachi City in the Tokyo Metropolis, 10 cities in Ibaraki Prefecture, four locations in Saitama Prefecture and two in Chiba Prefecture.

‌



The JMA said there was no threat of a tsunami.

‌



Kurumi Mori, a foreign correspondent at the BBC, wrote in a post on X: "Earthquake alert went off on my phones — followed by shaking in Tokyo Magnitude 5.9 in Ibaraki prefecture (next to Tokyo) at 2:02am. No tsunami warning." Describing the sound of the alert, she added in a follow-up post in Japanese: "No matter how many times I hear it, it really startles me."

View 2 Images The epicentre of the earthquake was in the south of the Ibaraki Prefecture (Image: Japan Meteorological Agency)
