World.title: Three people injured in shooting in Fort Smith, N.W.T.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Three people were injured in a shooting outside a business in Fort Smith, N.W.T., early Saturday morning, RCMP have confirmed.

The incident happened as the opening event of the Fireweed Festival was drawing to a close in the community of just over 2,000 people situated on the Slave River next to the Alberta border.

A shelter-in-place order was in effect as of noon on Saturday, as police searched for the shooter.

Fort Smith Mayor Dana Fergusson asked the community to remain calm, follow the directions of police, and to not share misinformation.

“Just hang in there and be strong because we know what a beautiful, great and amazing community we are,” she said. “This isn’t us and this isn't what represents us.”

Fergusson was in the parking lot with her son outside Dirty O'Fergies bar when the incident took place. The bar, located in the Pelican Rapids Inn, is owned by her family.

“We were escorting people off the property like, you know, 'Hey, time to go, night's over,' that kind of thing. And it happened right in front of us,” said Fergusson. “It just happened very quickly.”

What started as an altercation between a group of men resulted in multiple shots being fired, witnesses said.

Fergusson said she first went to help the injured, along with two staff members, before getting everyone else on the scene back into the safety of the building until emergency responders arrived.

What started the altercation is currently unconfirmed but Fergusson insisted the shooting was not representative of her community.

“It's just sad because it didn't need to be this way,” she said. “It’s not the community, it's these bad apples bringing their bad energy.”

As police searched for the suspect, the RCMP issued a shelter in place order around 3 a.m. MT, reissuing it just before 8 a.m. MT to include For Smith, Bell Rock and Sawmill Island.

The three injured people are receiving medical attention, police said, without giving information on their identities.

Police describe the suspect as male with a heavy build, medium complexion, black hair and facial hair, wearing a gray sweater. He is believed to be armed.

The suspect is described by police as male with a heavy build, medium complexion, black hair and facial hair, wearing a gray sweater. (RCMP)

One of the organizers of the Fireweed Festival, Melissa Faith-Johns, told CBC she is “devastated.”

“I put my blood, sweat and tears into this festival. To have someone take that in a moment,” she said. “We have people here from all over Canada.”

Festival organizers were still waiting for direction from police on what will happen with the festival for the rest of the weekend, she said. The Park Party originally planned at Queen Elizabeth Territorial Park has been postponed. Further updates would be posted to the Festival's Facebook page.

People are asked to contact police if they have information on the shooting. Police have opened a community portal for the public to collect digital evidence from witnesses.

Just before 8 a.m. MT on Aug. 22, the RCMP issued an updated image of the suspect, wanted after an active shooter event in Fort Smith. (RCMP)

Residents are advised to stay in their homes and not open the door for anyone, as well as refrain from posting photos of responding officers on social media.

The Fort Smith Health Centre is open for emergency access only, and is under lockdown. A mass casualty protocol was lifted at 7.45 a.m. MT, but the health authority said the lockdown will remain in effect until police advise it is safe to return to normal operations. Residents are asked to call ahead if possible before seeking care.

The Fort Smith Community and Recreation Centre is also closed until the shelter-in-place order is lifted.

In its fifth year, the Fireweed Festival NT is a music, culture and community festival. It includes live performances, interactive workshops and community-driven events in what organizers describe as an "inclusive and welcoming space."

World.title: Israeli settler blockades part of escalating violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The recent siege of Palestinian homes by militant Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra in the occupied West Bank is far from an isolated incident.

But the U.S. citizenship of one of the Palestinian homeowners has drawn more media attention than the near-daily acts of aggression by hardline Jewish settlers aimed at pushing Palestinians from their land typically receive.

Ohio-based businessman Loui Ridi returned to Qusra on Monday, August 17, to protect his home – and his brother and nephew, who live there — as settlers encircled it and two nearby homes.

"I called my brother and he said, 'I have no food. I don't want to leave the house, but I need food,'" Ridi told CBC news in a video call from Qusra after his arrival.

For them to leave, he said, would be to invite the settlers to take his home.

WATCH | Palestinian-American pleads for U.S. to help end Israeli settler siege:

"Just two months ago [settlers] were at my neighbour's village in Jalud," he said. "They put a siege on the family for a couple of weeks. And unfortunately, they managed to kick them out of their own house."

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law. They have expanded significantly under the current government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ultranationalist coalition partners, who critics accuse of giving tacit approval to settler violence.

One of Ridi's first acts after returning to Qusra was to fly an American flag from the roof of his building. He's asked the U.S. Embassy for help.

Qusra is about 16 kilometres south of Nablus as the crow flies and is surrounded by settlement blocs, including Migdalim and Shilo, as well as a growing number of outposts occupied by radical settlers.

Settler attacks causing casualties or property damage are averaging about six incidents a day this year, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs — "higher than in any year on record."

LISTEN | Palestinian-American returns to Qusra as Israeli settler violence surges in West Bank: The Current 24:11 American-Palestinian trapped in West Bank amid Israeli settler siege We hear from Loui Ridi who travelled from Ohio to the village of Qusra in the West Bank to help his brother and nephew who have been trapped in their home, after Israeli settlers surrounded their house last week. Then political analyst, Dahlia Scheindlin, on what this situation means in the larger context of surging Israeli settler violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank, and where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government stands on the issue.

The violence in Qusra prompted a rebuke from the U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who denounced those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" on social media.

"We're appalled at some of the things that have happened to families who are the victims of just criminal activity that is inexcusable and repugnant," he told Reuters in a later televised interview.

"I don't call them settlers," he said. "They're un-settlers."

Huckabee is a strong supporter of Israel's settlement policy and of Jewish claims to a biblical right to the land, referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria.

More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem. Many live in large, long-established blocs, while others live in unauthorized outposts considered illegal even under Israeli law, at least on paper.

Huckabee has dismissed violent settlers as a small minority.

Critics say that ignores what they describe as a de-facto institutional annexation of the West Bank that increasingly relies on violence.

A young Palestinian boy is seen at a mosque allegedly burned by Israeli settlers in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 26. Palestinian officials said Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques in the occupied West Bank overnight on July 26, after this week's deadly clashes in the territory left six people dead. Violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has surged since the Gaza war began with Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. (John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images)

"I think Mr Huckabee is missing the main point," said Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, an Israeli NGO that monitors Israeli settlements.

"The problem is not the specific house in Qusra. The problem is the system which produces this type of violence," he said.

"The idea that Israel can rule three million Palestinians in the West Bank through its military while more and more land is being grabbed and given to Israeli settlers."

At Qusra, Israeli border police and units from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) were deployed. The IDF said the forces were deployed to restore order and remove settlers blockading the Palestinian homes.

"IDF and Border Police forces acted to restore order and remove the Israeli Civilians from the area," an IDF statement said. It also said illegal structures erected in the area had been removed and that troops would remain.

Ridi said IDF soldiers declared the area around his home a closed military zone and urged him to stay inside, while allowing one settler to approach his property and intimidate him.

"I told the IDF guy, or the soldier, even though it's a military zone. I'm on my property…. Your job, you were sent here to move that settler and arrest him."

On Friday, Reuters published a video apparently filmed by Ridi showing an Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

WATCH | Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra: Israeli soldiers appear to throw items from balcony of besieged house in West Bank's Qusra | Duration 3:23 Video obtained by Reuters, filmed by Palestinian-American Loui Ridi, that appears to show one Israeli soldier throwing items from the balcony of one of the besieged houses in Qusra and another dumping things into a well on the property.

For Palestinians, scenes like those contribute to an increasingly blurred line between soldiers and settlers. IDF units operating in the West Bank can include ideological settlers, and the military also trains settler security units.

The IDF referred a query from CBC News about whether any Israelis had been arrested in connection with the Qusra blockade to Israeli police, who have not responded.

The fact that the settlers have not been permanently removed has fuelled a belief among Palestinians that the IDF is there to enable Israel's settlement enterprise.

"Because if the Israeli army wants to move the settlers they can move [them] in just one hour," said Rabia Odeh, 22, another Qusra resident who lives on the other side of the village from Ridi.

"But the settlers and the Israeli army are playing together, just in front of our eyes."

Israeli settlers and people in military uniforms stand outside a Palestinian's house in Qusra, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, in this screengrab taken from a handout video released August 10. (Reuters)

CBC News first met Odeh in the fall of 2023 after her family's home was attacked by militant settlers from a nearby outpost on a hill overlooking Qusra.

They threw rocks at the house and set cars outside it on fire.

Four Palestinians were killed in the confrontation that followed. Two more men from the village were killed during their funeral.

Odeh says the outpost has grown since then.

Now married and expecting her first child, she lives in a home equipped with exterior security cameras.

"Even when I have to go to my mother's house I check the cameras," she said. "So if the settlers [are] outside, I can't go outside."

Both Odeh's former and current homes are on the outskirts of Qusra, as is Ridi's.

"What we see happening in the past month is that this violence is targeted more and more to the outskirts of Palestinian built-up areas," said Etkes.

"To reduce the area where Palestinians can live, where Palestinians move," he said.

Settlement watch groups say the strategy is aimed at pushing Palestinians into smaller areas and making it easier to connect settlement blocs and outposts across different parts of the West Bank.

"Qusra, this is probably, you know, one of the best examples of what we have seen in the last month," said Etkes. "But this is not something which happens only in Qusra. This is happening also in dozens of other Palestinian villages in the West Bank."

Settlement expansion is also continuing on a much larger scale elsewhere.

On Thursday, Canada joined France, Germany, the United Kingdom and several other countries in condemning Israel's decision to publish construction tenders for a new settlement known as E1, just outside occupied East Jerusalem.

"The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian Territories," said a joint statement.

World.title: Lunenburg to La-La Land: Logan Taylor chases lifelong NFL dream
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Before Logan Taylor's 10th birthday, he was already over six feet tall, dwarfing his opponents on the soccer field.

"I would always get fouls and penalties and everything for kind of being too rough out there, so yeah, I definitely stood out when it came to size," said the now 24-year-old Nova Scotian who grew up in Lunenburg.

Taylor said one day a coach of a local football team had a conversation with his dad.

"He was like, 'Hey, you got to get your son out here,'" said Taylor. "And from the day I stepped onto the football field, I loved the team aspect and I just loved the contact, so it was just a great fit for me and [I'm] just very thankful that I got that opportunity.”

Fast-forward to today and the six-foot-seven-inch, 312-pound offensive lineman is living in Los Angeles going through his first training camp with the NFL's Chargers, months after being selected in the sixth round of the NFL Draft. He's the highest-selected born and raised Nova Scotian taken in the NFL Draft.

Taylor runs a drill at the NFL scouting combine in Indianapolis on March 1, 2026. (Michael Conroy/AP)

It's the culmination of a lifelong dream that meant moving away at 14 from his home in the tiny seaside South Shore community. This has included stops in Timberlea, N.S., Virginia and Massachusetts to chase his dream.

While Nova Scotia has produced hockey stars such as Sidney Crosby and Nathan MacKinnon, the list of born-and-raised Bluenosers who have played in a regular-season game in the NFL is a short one: Tyrone Williams and Steve Morley.

Because the high school in Bridgewater, N.S., he was supposed to attend did not have a football program, Taylor moved to Timberlea for his grades 10 and 11 years to attend what was then known as Sir John A. Macdonald High School.

Kathy and Brian Mason were his billet parents. Brian Mason said when Taylor arrived to live with them, he would've been about six feet six inches and 280 pounds, so he physically stood out. He recalls hearing some people dismiss Taylor's goal of reaching the NFL.

"And we told him, like, 'Don't listen to them. It's within you to make it and you have to put in the work to get there,'" said Brian Mason.

Houston Texans defensive end Solomon Byrd, right, collides with Chargers guard Logan Taylor in the first quarter of an NFL pre-season game in Houston on Aug. 13, 2026. (Maria Lysaker/AP)

The Masons describe Taylor as a gentle giant, caring, humble and respectful.

Kathy Mason said that Taylor was open to having conversations and seeing a different point of view.

"There were some challenges, but nothing that we hadn't seen before with our own [two] boys," she said.

Taylor is shown with his 'Timberlea parents,' Kathy and Brian Mason, in a photo from when he lived with them when he was in Grade 10. (Submitted by Kathy Mason)

Taylor said that moving away at 14, "I had to grow up really fast." He said the Masons are two of his four parents.

For his Grade 12 year, Taylor attended a boarding school in Virginia. For his first two years of post-secondary studies, he attended the University of Virginia. His final three were at Boston College.

For the NFL Draft in April, Taylor was at home in Lunenburg. The Masons were also there, although they hadn't arrived when he got the phone call from the Chargers.

Taylor is from Lunenburg, a small, picturesque town on Nova Scotia's South Shore. (Andrew Vaughan/The Canadian Press)

"It was just an amazing feeling," said Taylor. "To be able to be there with my parents and my wife and her family was just an amazing experience."

Taylor spoke with CBC News by video recently from the Chargers' practice facility days ahead of the team's second pre-season exhibition game.

Life in L.A.

He said on a typical day he's up before 6 a.m. PT. There are team meetings starting at 7 a.m. and they usually run two hours. There's a practice from 10 a.m. to noon, a lunch break and then more team meetings in the afternoon. In the evening, there's a non-contact practice known as a walk-through.

"You're going against the best of the best in practice and then when you get to the game, it's a whole other level," said Taylor.

He said he's enjoying his time living in Los Angeles, singling out the lack of rain and abundance of beaches and restaurants as highlights, but as a "country guy," he hasn't been able to do his usual pursuits: four-wheeling, hunting and fishing.

"But hey, I'm here for my job," said Taylor.

The Chargers selected four offensive linemen in the draft, meaning Taylor has his work cut out for him to land on the 53-man active roster.

Taylor sits on the bench during the second half of a 2023 NCAA college football game against Northern Illinois in Boston. (Michael Dwyer/AP)

Brian Mason said he told Taylor that being drafted just means the door opened for him.

"Now you can step in, but this is where the work begins. You have to show them that you belong and you have to put in the hard work to stay there and prove yourself," said Mason.

"And he goes, 'I know.' I said, 'So let's do it, let's just show them how tough a kid from Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, really is.'"

Taylor, who has helped with summer football camps back home, said he wants to be a resource for young Nova Scotians looking to play professional football.

Taylor (65) leads Boston College onto the field prior to a game against California on Sept. 27, 2025. (Greg M. Cooper/AP)

Asked what advice he has for them, his answer applies equally to his current situation.

"The days that you're like, 'Oh, I don't really want to,' those are the days someone else is [going to put in the hard work]," said Taylor.

"So just have that mindset of, yeah, if you're not going to do it, well, someone else will. And someone's always coming for your job, so just attack every single day."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Visitors outfoxed by footwear thieves at provincial park in Sask.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Cunning and furry thieves are outfoxing campers and cottagers at Great Blue Heron Provincial Park.

Sonnet McGuire, manager of the park located about 50 kilometres north of Prince Albert, says she started getting reports about shoes going missing in early July.

Visitors found single shoes left in bushes, on the side of the road, or even at the boat launch.

The culprits: a group — sometimes known as a skulk — of sly foxes with a taste for footwear.

“We have five foxes that are moving about the campground and they seem to love stealing people's shoes,” McGuire said.

The behaviour isn’t new, but this year the thieves are more active.

“We knew it was gonna be foxes because we've had this before, the odd time, just not to this level,” McGuire said.

At first, the park kept the lost shoes in the back of the campground office, but it quickly had to upgrade to outdoor storage bins to hold them. So many shoes.

Dozens of Crocs, flip flops, runners and Birkenstocks were stolen by the foxes and returned to the campground office to wait for their rightful owners. (Aishah Ashraf/CBC)

McGuire said there were about 70 in the bin on a recent day, but she suspects over 100 have passed through it this summer.

“It's kind of like a scavenger hunt in the campground because as you're walking around the campground on the trail or wherever you might be, people are just finding shoes," she said.

“We had one story where people were walking down the street and they saw one fox sitting on the road and the other one kind of on the edge of the campsite. And it was almost like the one fox was on lookout and the other one went into the campsite, stole a shoe, and then they both took off running.”

WATCH | A fox took your shoe? Get in line at this Sask. campground: A fox took your shoe? Get in line at this Sask. campground | Duration 2:26 Five foxes at Saskatchewan's Great Blue Heron Provincial Park have gotten their paws on more than 100 shoes this summer — turning the campground lost-and-found into a growing collection of stolen footwear.

Camper Brenda Andres said she’s also seen the furry criminals at work.

“We just turned onto the first highway and a little fox ran across the road, and sure enough, he had a little shoe in his mouth,” Andres said.

She’ll be keeping her shoes inside during her camping trip.

One of the shoe-swiping foxes caught in the act in the Sunnyside subdivision at Emma Lake. (Doreen Smuda/Facebook)

‘Kind of a fun game’

Cottager Rachelle Kelln doesn’t mind the sneaky visitors.

“It's kind of a fun game,” she said.

Her cottage is in the Carwin Park subdivision near Emma Lake. It’s also a favourite dumping ground for the shoe-swiping foxes.

“We just started noticing more and more shoes,” Kelln said.

She’s found at least six on her property since July 10, and even more left on the side of the road — all types of shoes, including flip flops, Birkenstocks, even Adidas Sambas.

“Those are expensive shoes and there's a bit of panic around those ones,” Kelln said.

She’s had a few people stop by to pick up their shoes, and they’ve all been excited to get back on the right foot.

McGuire said visitors to the park are advised to keep their kicks inside, as the foxy thieves will remain at large.

World.title: Tragically Hip band members reflect on Gord Downie and farewell tour 10 years after final show
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ten years after The Tragically Hip��’s emotional final concert, band members Paul Langlois and Rob Baker tell CBC’s Eli Glasner about how they remember that night in Kingston, Ont., and what grief looks like a decade after losing lead singer and friend, Gord Downie.

It’s been a decade since The Tragically Hip’s final concert in Kingston, Ont., but Paul Langlois feels he hasn’t fully processed it yet.

"It’s hard to believe it’s been 10 years since that last show, since our last show," the Tragically Hip guitarist said in an interview with CBC’s Eli Glasner, which aired on The National Thursday night.

"I’m just trying to be in a place of appreciation for what we did and how it seems to have affected people."

It was a bittersweet night as Hip lead singer and lyricist Gord Downie said goodbye to thousands packed into Kingston’s Rogers K-Rock Centre (now known as Slush Puppi Place) and millions watching across the country. Fans and Downie cried together as Downie sang hits like Ahead by a Century and Bobcaygeon for the last time.

Downie sings during the Tragically Hip's final show in Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (David Bastedo)

The Canadian band, which released 13 studio albums since its formation in 1984, toured for the final time in 2016. They capped it off with a show in their hometown on Aug. 20, 2016. Downie had been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer in Dec. 2015 and died just over a year later, aged 53.

CBC will rebroadcast the band’s final concert on Saturday to commemorate its 10th anniversary. You can find a list of screenings of The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration here.

WATCH | The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast: The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration | 10th Anniversary Rebroadcast COMING UP Relive the night Canada stood still for the live broadcast of The Tragically Hip’s 2016 Man Machine Poem concert from Kingston, Ont., re-broadcasting and streaming commercial-free on Saturday, August 22 on CBC TV, CBC Gem, CBC Radio and CBC Music’s YouTube page.

"I really appreciate that it matters to people, that people still care — about the band, the music, that they want to pay their respects to Gord in some way," said guitarist Rob Baker.

"It’s not so much a celebration for me, it’s a remembrance … the last show was the last day of a career that I loved."

Langlois recalls feeling uncomfortable and uneasy before the final performance.

"I went to the arena early, for some reason I was just kind of going a bit squirrely," he said. “It was starting to seep in that this is the last show, so I kind of had a heavy feeling."

But as soon as Downie showed up to the soundcheck, Langlois’s mood changed.

"[Downie] looked around and he's just like, 'This is going to be so great,'" Langlois recalled.

"It just changed me. I’m like, 'You think so?' and he’s like 'Yeah. It’s going to be so fun.' It lightened me up."

Downie is seen performing on a screen as a man in Vancouver watches during a viewing party for the final stop of The Tragically Hip's tour in Kingston. A decade on, band members said they had no idea how much the final show meant to Canadians until after. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Baker said he was focused on his friend and bandmate on the tour.

“I was there to support Gord, and to help Gord realize his last wish. He really wanted to do it again, and he wanted to look every last person in the arena in the eye, and make a connection, to say thank you to them.”

But Baker said it wasn’t always easy.

"I had to keep all of my emotions jammed down, corked down inside the bottle — much to my detriment later on. But I couldn’t have gotten through it otherwise," he said.

"There’s no way I’d get through it. You can’t stand on stage, blubbering. I had a job to do, and that’s to be attentive to where Gord’s going to take a song … and to be there to support him."

From left, Paul Langlois and Rob Baker speak with the CBC’s Eli Glasner at the Glenn Gould Theatre, in Toronto, on Tuesday. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

At first, the band members were worried that Downie’s condition would affect him on stage. But, they said, the singer seemed to improve physically throughout the farewell tour.

At the time, the band didn’t realize how big a deal their last show would be.

“I don’t think it crossed anyone’s mind that there might be big screens in a small town, or on a campground, or in someone’s backyard,” Langlois said.

People who couldn't get a ticket to the band's final show gather in Springer Market Square to listen to the Tragically Hip in downtown Kingston, Ont., on Aug. 20, 2016. (Lars Hagberg/The Canadian Press)

“It wasn’t really until the days after where I think we all started to realize, ‘Oh, that was maybe a bit bigger than we thought.’”

Baker and Langlois are emphatic that the band won’t be getting back together.

Hip release new album

But the band did release a new album on Friday, Live July 22 – August 20, 2016, which features recordings from across the 2016 tour.

Baker said the members of The Tragically Hip were always forward-looking, so putting together an album of past performances was difficult at times.

But, Baker added, music can have a healing quality.

He recalled when he burst into tears at a remembrance of life for Downie’s father, Edgar, who died in 2015. He later told Downie he felt it happened because he hadn’t grieved when his own parents died.

"And [Downie] said, ‘You’re so full of shit. I see you up on the bus at four o’clock in the morning listening to Artie Shaw, or Benny Goodman or something.’ He said, ‘What do you think you’re doing?'" Baker said. "I was like, 'You’re absolutely right.' I didn’t think I was grieving, but of course I was."

“Music helps you through things. Sometimes you have no idea it’s even happening.”

World.title: Canadians like to think we're nice. But loaning my car to a stranger made me question what that really means
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person is the experience of Manon Christensen, who lives in Barrie, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

My daughter, Anna, had just passed her road test and we were waiting for the paperwork when we overheard the conversation next to us.

“We cannot provide a car for your road test,” a clipped voice informed the man at the driving test centre counter.

The man’s shoulders sagged. The woman on the other side softened, letting her dispassionate clerk mask slip.

“I’m sorry,” she said, “You’ll have to rent one.’’

The man said he had no money to do so and they were at an impasse.

Anna levelled me with a stare that said: "We have a car. He does not."

I sighed. Teen math.

The truth is that there is something uniquely Canadian about wanting to appear helpful without becoming meaningfully involved. We are nice. At least we’re very attached to the idea of ourselves that way. We also mind our own business, which means not admitting to eavesdropping. And we definitely don’t interfere.

But lending my car to a stranger? That hit differently. Liability. Risk. Inconvenience. The kind of thing sensible people know better than to do.

Anna’s eyebrows arched, waiting to see whom I would choose to be at that moment.

I don’t mentally switch places with people as much anymore. Somewhere along the way, I have learned to insulate myself from uncomfortable feelings. To emote less. It’s easier that way. As a born-and-raised Canadian, I’m good at the nothing-to-see-here game.

But for a moment, I let myself imagine being him. To be new to this country. I saw myself on my own moving to France, Japan and Kenya — in all the places I have felt out of my depth.

He started to leave.

I stepped out of line.

We introduced ourselves to Godwin, who immigrated from Nigeria less than a year ago. He took driving lessons, rented a car and failed his first attempt. He hadn’t been behind a wheel since. His next road test was the next day. A licence would mean more work options, he said.

I thought about all the other ways I wanted to spend an evening after work, but I told him that he could use my car for his test.

He was thankful and then searched my face.

“Will you really come, Manon?”

Anna and I decided to take him on the route she had just completed for her test.

In the car, Godwin fully reclined his seat before working out how to slide it back. He took slow, deep breaths, yet when he veered out of the parking space, he came close to striking a pedestrian. I wondered if I was putting all of our lives at risk, but Godwin started to pick up speed and I bit my lip.

He was so eager for feedback — unlike Anna. When he attempted a three-point turn, he signalled in all the wrong directions. I told Godwin to keep driving after he completed the circuit. He gained confidence. He told us what it was like living in Lagos. He described the relentless pulse of a city of 20 million people and the fierce competition for jobs. He missed home, but spoke about Canada with determined optimism.

Christensen, centre, with her daughter, Anna, right, who was not eager for feedback for her driving test and Godwin, left, who wanted to soak in the advice. (Submitted by Manon Christensen)

We met the next day.

His examiner approached at a determined pace. Her face was settled into a deep frown. She snapped at me when I handed him the keys: “Don’t interfere.’’

Too late for that.

I was pacing outside the driving test centre when I got a call 20 minutes later. I could only hear hysterics on the other end. High-pitched, unintelligible sounds.

I pictured Godwin in a car wreck — my car wreck. The call went dead. I wondered what catastrophe had unfolded: twisted metal, horrified examiner, insurance claims. Each passing second fed my imagination.

Then I spotted Godwin, arms spread wide, striding through the crowded parking lot like a king. He was lit from within. His chest heaved and his breaths were syncopated. He picked me up in a bear hug.

I wasn't quite sure how to reciprocate and felt rather limp.

The sight we must have made. Me, middle-aged and awkward, enfolded in the arms of a young, jubilant man. We were not pulling off the nothing-to-see-here Canadian vibe very well.

Yet his light caught: joy sparked in me before I could name it.

Then it all tumbled out. He was terrible, he admitted — barely a pass, but he must have done just enough right.

“I can now count you my friend forever, Manon.”

Well, then.

Godwin and Manon for the win.

As I waved goodbye, I realized that this was exactly where I hadn’t known I wanted to be today. The nervous anticipation, the awkward hug, the burst of pride I hadn’t expected to feel. Most friendships don’t begin in parking lots.

Christensen, right, with her daughter, Anna, who taught her the difference between being nice and being good. (Submitted by Manon Christensen)

On my drive home, I saw it. Anna had wordlessly reminded me that there is a difference between being nice and being good. Wishing people well is easy. Goodness makes room for them. One costs little; the other asks something of us.

Kids these days.

I might just have a thing or two to learn from them.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: A grim property search, 3 grieving families and 'a lot of questions' in this eastern Ontario area
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Earlier this week, police announced the remains of a third man, Lawrence Bertrim, had been found on a rural property north of the normally quiet eastern Ontario town of Smiths Falls.

Mayor Shawn Pankow said news of the discovery earlier this month was likely met with mixed emotions: While there's hope someone who's gone missing, as Bertrim did nearly four years ago, will one day come home alive, learning of a death is an opportunity to give him the dignity he deserves and provide "some degree of closure."

It's the latest grim finding on a densely wooded, 16-hectare lot located off Kelly Jordan Road in Montague, a township hugging Smiths Falls, which is about 80 kilometres southwest of Ottawa.

The town of Smiths Falls, which has about 9,000 residents, is just south of where the remains of the three men were found. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Two weeks earlier, the remains of Robert Lambert, who'd been missing even longer, were recovered.

Nine months before that, the remains of Robbie Thomson, who was last seen three years ago, were found. Three people have been charged in Thomson's death; a fourth is charged with being an accessory to the killing.

However, no one's been charged in the suspicious deaths of Bertrim and Lambert as rewards of $50,000 are being offered for useful information.

Although the three men's remains were found at the same site, police aren't explicitly linking their deaths.

They're also asking the public to give police officers the space and time needed to investigate the case and bring resolution to Bertrim's and Lambert's families.

"We need to remember that there are families impacted by these deaths," Sgt. Erin Cranton, a spokesperson for Ontario Provincial Police (OPP), which is leading all three investigations, said Wednesday outside the service's east region headquarters in Smiths Falls.

"I think it's important that the public take a step back, recognize that there are people that are grieving and trying to accept some closure maybe. And just let us do our job.

"We are doing everything we can to bring answers."

'Quite the graveyard'

Smiths Falls, which has about 9,000 residents, is typically in the regional news for its economic ups and downs related to the Hershey's chocolate factory and, more recently, a cannabis producer.

The community isn't used to the periodic jolts coming out of the unfolding scene off Kelly Jordan Road.

On Wednesday, Radio-Canada interviewed one person in downtown Smiths Falls who remarked that the site appeared to be " quite the graveyard."

"It's not something we've really ever been through before," Pankow said in his own interview, noting that Bertrim was last seen in the downtown area that includes the mayor's office.

Mayor Shawn Pankow, shown outside the town hall in Smiths Falls in 2023, says of the discovery of the men's remains: 'It's not something we've really ever been through before.' (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

In 2023, the disappearances of Bertrim and Thomson had people on edge, creating speculation that police sought to tamp down.

Pankow said that anxiety diminished in the wake of the charges last year against the four accused in the Thomson case.

"We expect charges coming on the other two [cases]," the mayor said. "And so the fear of some other culprit being out there or risk to other citizens is probably drying up."

But Cranton said there's still more work to do.

"In this case, we need to determine what the linkages were and what led to the deaths," she said.

"We understand there are a lot of questions. We have to ensure that we do the most thorough investigation possible."

OPP Sgt. Erin Cranton says the police force knows the public has a lot of questions about the case involving the discovery of the remains of three men at the same property. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

As families and the community await answers, here's a timeline of how things have unfolded:

2004

Lambert, of Montague Township, purchases the property off Kelly Jordan Road, according to property records obtained by CBC last year. He was 75 when he disappeared in the summer of 2018.

Robert Lambert was 75 when he went missing in 2018. He's seen in a photo shared by OPP at the time. (Ontario Provincial Police/Facebook)

Decades earlier, Lambert moved to the Smiths Falls area from the U.S. to be with his future wife, Kathryn Lambert.

Her son has described Robert as a loving and caring husband, and said Kathryn's death in 2016 was "a struggle for him to overcome."

2018

April: Christopher Fenton, one of the four men charged in Thomson's death, becomes a co-owner of the Kelly Jordan Road property.

Lambert was the sole owner of this house on the Kelly Jordan Road property until April 2018, when Christopher Fenton, one of the people now accused of murdering Lambert, came on as co-owner. (Ontario Provincial Police/Facebook)

Lambert disappears soon after.

July: The month Lambert went missing, according to OPP.

At the time of his disappearance, investigators were told Lambert had returned to the U.S., OPP said, adding there was no record of Lambert crossing the border.

Police would publicly report Lambert as missing four months later. By January 2019, they were "increasingly concerned" about the circumstances of his disappearance.

2022

Sept. 30: Bertrim, of Smiths Falls, is last seen. He was 42 when he was reported as missing on Oct. 2.

"I know that people are hearing things and have information," Bertrim's mother, Linda Young, later said in a video appeal released by OPP. "Help bring my family some closure."

Lawrence Bertrim was the second of the three men to disappear, but his remains were the last to be found. (OPP handout)

2023

February: OPP join the investigation into Bertrim's disappearance, led by the Smiths Falls Police Service.

Oct. 12-18: Thomson, who according to OPP was known to frequent Smiths Falls and Prescott, goes missing. Police are told about his disappearance on Oct. 19.

Thomson and Bertrim knew each other, as CBC would later learn.

Thomson, 34, was the youngest of the three men who went missing.

Robbie Thomson, whose remains were found in October, went missing in 2023. (OPP handout)

Thomson's family has described him as a gentle giant who stood up for his Junior B hockey teammates and was always willing to lend a hand around the house.

"Normally he'd be in contact with either me or my dad every three days. Within five days, there was nothing," his sister, Tabatha Thomson, said of his disappearance.

Nov. 3: Steven Tate, a 34-year-old from Montague Township, is reported missing after he was last seen that day.

It's believed Thomson and Bertrim knew Tate.

The body of Steve Tate was found adjacent to Highway 15, which cuts through Smiths Falls, in November 2023. (OPP)

Nov. 8: Tate's body is discovered in a ditch along Highway 15, which cuts through Smiths Falls.

Later in the month, OPP say they believe Tate was the victim of a hit-and-run. That same day, they issue a separate release again appealing for information about the disappearances of Thomson and Bertrim.

Back then, police didn't connect those disappearances to Tate's, and aren't doing so now.

"At this time, we are not linking any of these investigations until we have the facts to do so," Cranton said Wednesday.

WATCH | People in Smiths Falls deal with the discovery of human remains on a property:

String of disappearances in Smith Falls, Ont. has left some residents feeling ‘unnerved’ | Duration 2:09 Some residents in Smith Falls, Ont. said they want more information from police about the recent string of disappearances of three men in the area over the past year, including one whose body was found earlier this week.

2024

Sept. 10: OPP report they have conducted a number of searches and followed up on numerous tips from the public.

"While there have been multiple appeals for information, investigators still believe someone has a key piece of evidence that will help determine what happened to Lawrence Bertrim and Robbie Thomson."

In 2024, police released this photo of a drone to illustrate their ongoing efforts to find Bertrim and Thomson. (OPP)

2025

Oct. 29: OPP arrest (and soon after charge) three people in the death of Thomson — including Christopher Fenton, who co-owns the Kelly Jordan Road property alongside Lambert, who'd long gone missing.

Fenton, 48, and Erin Mackie, 40, both from Montague Township, and 34-year-old Joshua Belfiori of Kingston are accused of first-degree murder.

Thomson's father tells CBC the charges brings some solace, but he hopes police will find his boy's remains.

"There's a big void," he says.

In August, an OPP vehicle blocks off the entrance to the property where the remains were found. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Oct. 30: Officers find Thomson's remains while executing a search warrant at the Kelly Jordan Road property — the first in what would prove to be a trio of upsetting but clarifying discoveries at the site over the next nine months.

"I didn't think we'd get him back," Thomson's sister, Tabatha Thomson, says after learning the news, which was announced by the OPP on Nov. 5, after the remains were identified and the family was notified.

"It is important that [families] know first when a loved one is found," Cranton said Wednesday.

WATCH | Robbie Thomson's family reacts to the charges: Charges bring some relief for family of Smiths Falls man missing for two years | Duration 2:20 OPP have charged three people with first-degree murder in the death of a Smiths Falls, Ont., man reported missing two years ago.

Oct. 31: Robert Lambert's family tells CBC that they still hope to get answers that have been "a long time coming."

"The entire area of Smiths Falls has been ... holding [its] breath for years now."

2026

March 19: Erin Mackie, one of three people accused of murdering Thomson, is denied bail.

Bail proceedings for one of the accused in Thomson's death took place at the Perth, Ont., courthouse earlier this year. (Joseph Tunney/CBC)

July 20: Nine months after Thomson's remains were found, Lambert's remains are recovered from the Montague Township property (announced by OPP on Aug. 5).

Aug. 6: Bertrim's remains are also located on the property, as disclosed by the OPP on Aug. 18.

"Of course, we can't time when we're going to make a discovery in terms of the investigation," Cranton tells CBC.

"We obviously went through a winter period during our search efforts. So that does change the ability to manoeuvre around the property, [which] is a large property."

Pankow, who attended Thomson's memorial last year, said there's an expectation "this is all tied together" and that further charges will come.

"But we know police have to do their due diligence. They'll work their way through, and I think that day will come."

Cranton said OPP are still seeking information in all three investigations, adding that the $50,000 rewards for useful tips in the Lawrence and Bertrim cases remain in place.

Police tape marks the Kelly Jordan Road property on Tuesday. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

Aug. 20: OPP decline to say if they believe there could be other people's remains on the property, or whether they're even searching for other bodies.

"Police will maintain an increased presence on Kelly Jordan Road," they said in their Aug. 18 release.

Pankow said he views the investigation as "an anomaly" for his town.

"The reality is, we're a safe community," he said Wednesday. "A lot of good things happen here. We're fortunate.

"I still hear some people say, 'We don't even bother locking our doors at night.'"

World.title: Read Mark Carney’s full statement on the collapse of trade talks with the U.S.
World.content:
Our objectives in our trade negotiations have been to:

Preserve tariff-free access to the U.S. for the vast majority of Canadian business;

Provide greater stability to our trade relationship;

Significantly reduce U.S. tariffs on our key strategic industries, so that Canadian businesses in these sectors would have the best access of any in the world;

Protect our small and medium-sized businesses – the lifeblood of our economy – including by removing the imminent threat of new tariffs; and

Maintain our flexibility, independence, and sovereignty so we can keep building the Canada we want.

We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship. Our government understood, before many, that America is altering all its trade relationships. Putting tariffs on its closest allies and charging for access to its vast market.

We have worked in that context. To strike a fair deal that would provide the best access to the U.S. market and greater certainty to Canadian businesses and workers. Throughout, our goal has been to secure the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any deadline.

In recent weeks, we made important progress toward improving Canada’s position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S.

However, that progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians. As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa. They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute. However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.

At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.

In the coming days, the government will introduce additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses, building on the nearly $25 billion in support provided over the past 18 months.

These actions complement Canada’s core economic strategy. From day one, we have been focused on building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.

That strategy is working. We are advancing nearly $500 billion in major infrastructure projects. In parallel, we are unlocking new export markets for Canadian businesses. Our existing free trade deals already provide Canada with preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers, and we are on track to double that market access by the end of this year.

Canadian economic growth is accelerating, and we are on course to have the second-fastest growth in the G7 over the next two years. Our economy is creating jobs at four times the rate of the United States. Our exports to non-U.S. markets are on track to double over the next decade. Foreign direct investment in Canada is at its highest level in two decades, running at twice the rate of our nearest G7 competitor. Canada now ranks as the most attractive country in the world for infrastructure investment.

Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future. We will set our own course to keep building Canada strong for all.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress
